title: The East India Company in India
subtitle: From a London trading company to the ruler of India · 1600 – 1874
subject: east-india-company
intro: Chartered in London in 1600 to trade spices, the East India Company spent its first 150 years as one of several European traders at the edges of the Mughal world, with fortified factories at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta. Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) turned it into the ruler of Bengal. Over the next century, by war, subsidiary alliances and annexation, it defeated Mysore, the Marathas and the Sikhs and governed most of the subcontinent — until the revolt of 1857 led the British Crown to take India over.

events.title: Royal charter
events.summary: Elizabeth I grants a group of London merchants a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. The East India Company's early target is the spice trade of the East Indies, not India.

events.title: Battle of Swally — a foothold at Surat
events.summary: Company ships defeat a Portuguese squadron off Surat. Jahangir's court, impressed, allows the English a factory (trading post) at Surat, the Mughal empire's chief port.

events.title: Sir Thomas Roe at Jahangir's court
events.summary: James I's ambassador spends four years following the Mughal court to secure better trading terms. The Company is still a petitioner, one trader among many.

events.title: Amboyna: pushed out of the spice islands
events.summary: The Dutch execute English traders at Amboyna in the Moluccas. Squeezed out of the spice trade, the Company turns to Indian cotton textiles, indigo and saltpetre.

events.title: Madras and Fort St. George
events.summary: Under a grant issued in the name of the Vijayanagara emperor, Francis Day acquires a strip of the Coromandel coast. Fort St. George is completed in 1644 and the town of Madras grows around it.

events.title: Bombay leased to the Company
events.summary: Bombay, which came to Charles II in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry from Portugal, is leased to the Company for £10 a year. It replaces Surat — raided twice by Shivaji — as the Company's west coast base.

events.title: Child's War — defeat by the Mughals
events.summary: Under governor Sir Josiah Child the Company attacks Mughal shipping and ports. Aurangzeb's forces besiege Bombay and seize Company factories; the English must beg for pardon and pay a fine. Military conquest is shelved for half a century.

events.title: Job Charnock at Sutanuti — Calcutta
events.summary: Job Charnock re-establishes the Company's Bengal trading post at Sutanuti on the Hooghly. In 1698 the Company buys the rights to three villages — Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata — and builds Fort William: the beginnings of Calcutta.

events.title: Farrukhsiyar's farman
events.summary: The emperor Farrukhsiyar grants the Company duty-free trade in Bengal. Abuse of these privileges by Company servants trading privately becomes a long-running grievance of the Bengal nawabs.

events.title: Carnatic Wars with the French
events.summary: The British and French companies, under Dupleix on the French side, fight through Indian allies for control of the Carnatic. Robert Clive makes his name defending Arcot (1751); the French are decisively beaten at Wandiwash (1760).

events.title: Siraj-ud-Daulah takes Calcutta
events.summary: The young Nawab of Bengal, angered by fortification work and trade abuses, captures Calcutta. British prisoners die overnight in a cramped guardroom — the 'Black Hole', whose death toll was later greatly exaggerated in British accounts.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.summary: Clive retakes Calcutta and, having secretly agreed to make the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar the new nawab, defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey when much of the Nawab's army stays out of the fight. The Company becomes kingmaker in India's richest province.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.summary: Mir Qasim, the nawab who tried to curb Company abuses, allies with Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and Emperor Shah Alam II. The Company defeats all three.

events.title: The Diwani of Bengal
events.summary: By the Treaty of Allahabad, Shah Alam II grants the Company the right to collect the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Bengal's revenue now pays for the Company's trade and armies.

events.title: Anglo-Mysore Wars
events.summary: Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan, with modernised armies and rockets, fight four wars against the Company. Hyder reaches the outskirts of Madras (1769); Tipu is killed when Srirangapatna is stormed in 1799.

events.title: Great Bengal famine
events.summary: Drought, harsh revenue collection and hoarding combine in a famine that kills perhaps a third of Bengal's population — estimates run to many millions.

events.title: Regulating Act; Warren Hastings Governor-General
events.summary: Parliament begins to oversee the Company. Warren Hastings, governor of Bengal, becomes the first Governor-General, with authority over Madras and Bombay.

events.title: First Anglo-Maratha War
events.summary: The Company backs Raghunathrao's claim to be Peshwa and is defeated at Wadgaon (1779). The Treaty of Salbai restores the pre-war position.

events.title: Pitt's India Act
events.summary: A government Board of Control in London is set over the Company's directors: the start of dual Company–Crown government of India.

events.title: Impeachment of Warren Hastings
events.summary: Edmund Burke leads the impeachment of Hastings for corruption and abuse of power in a seven-year trial that becomes a public debate over the Company's conduct. Hastings is acquitted.

events.title: Permanent Settlement
events.summary: Lord Cornwallis fixes Bengal's land revenue in perpetuity with zamindars, creating a landlord class loyal to British rule while leaving cultivators exposed.

events.title: Wellesley's expansion
events.summary: Governor-General Richard Wellesley uses subsidiary alliances — Hyderabad 1798, the Peshwa at Bassein 1802 — and wars against Mysore and the Marathas. His brother Arthur wins at Assaye; the Company takes Delhi and the Mughal emperor under its protection.

events.title: End of the trade monopoly
events.summary: The Charter Act of 1813 ends the Company's monopoly of trade with India (keeping tea and China) and allows missionaries in. The Company is becoming a government more than a business.

events.title: Third Anglo-Maratha War — the Peshwa falls
events.summary: The last Peshwa, Bajirao II, is defeated and exiled; the Holkars, Shindes and Bhonsles become subordinate princely states. The Company is now the paramount power in India.

events.title: First Anglo-Burmese War
events.summary: A costly war in the east adds Assam, Manipur and Arakan to Company territory.

events.title: Sati abolished
events.summary: Governor-General William Bentinck outlaws sati in Bengal, after years of campaigning by reformers such as Ram Mohan Roy.

events.title: The Company stops trading
events.summary: The Charter Act of 1833 ends the Company's remaining commercial activities. It becomes purely an administrator of India on behalf of the Crown; the Governor-General of Bengal becomes Governor-General of India.

events.title: English education
events.summary: After Macaulay's notorious minute dismissing Indian learning, the Company directs its education funding to teaching in English — creating the English-educated class that later leads the nationalist movement.

events.title: First Anglo-Afghan War
events.summary: An invasion to install a friendly ruler in Kabul ends in the destruction of the retreating British-Indian army in January 1842.

events.title: Anglo-Sikh Wars — Punjab annexed
events.summary: After Ranjit Singh's death (1839) the Sikh Empire weakens. Two hard-fought wars end with the annexation of the Punjab in 1849; the boy maharaja Duleep Singh is exiled to Britain.

events.title: Dalhousie's annexations
events.summary: Under the Doctrine of Lapse Dalhousie annexes states whose rulers die without natural heirs — Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) — and in 1856 annexes Awadh for 'misgovernment', deposing Wajid Ali Shah.

events.title: The Phules' school for girls in Pune
events.summary: Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule open one of the first schools for girls run by Indians, in Pune — the start of their lifelong work against caste and gender discrimination.

events.title: First passenger train
events.summary: India's first passenger train runs from Bombay to Thane. Railways and the telegraph spread rapidly under Dalhousie.

events.title: Revolt of 1857
events.summary: After Mangal Pandey's attack on officers at Barrackpore in March, sepoys mutiny at Meerut and march to Delhi, proclaiming Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor. The uprising spreads across north India — Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi — led by figures such as Nana Sahib, Rani Lakshmibai and Tatya Tope, and is crushed with great brutality.

events.title: The Crown takes over
events.summary: The Government of India Act transfers the Company's territories, army and powers to the British Crown. The Governor-General becomes Viceroy.

events.title: The Company is dissolved
events.summary: With its remaining dividend obligations paid off, the East India Company is formally wound up.
